facts.title: Your Brain as a Control Center
facts.body: The brain is the main control center of the nervous system. It processes senses, movement, memory, and emotion. Different regions specialize in different jobs.

facts.title: The Heart Never Truly Rests
facts.body:
The heart is a muscular pump that moves blood through the body. It has four chambers that guide blood in a one-way path. Its rhythmic contractions are coordinated by electrical signals.

Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to tissues. A healthy heart is central to overall health.

facts.title: Lungs and the Exchange of Breath
facts.body: The lungs bring oxygen into the body and remove carbon dioxide. Air travels through branching tubes to tiny air sacs called alveoli. Gas exchange happens across very thin surfaces. Breathing is assisted by the diaphragm and chest muscles.

facts.title: Blood the Body’s Transport River
facts.body:
Blood is a fluid tissue that carries gases, nutrients, wastes, and signals. Red blood cells transport oxygen using hemoglobin. White blood cells help defend against infection.

Platelets assist with clotting after injury. Plasma carries dissolved substances through the body.

facts.title: Bones Form a Living Framework
facts.body:
Bones support the body and protect vital organs. They store minerals such as calcium and phosphorus. Bone marrow helps make blood cells.

Bones are living tissues that are constantly rebuilt. Joints allow bones to move in coordinated ways.

facts.title: Muscles Create Motion
facts.body: Muscles allow movement, posture, and heat production. Skeletal muscles attach to bones and act under voluntary control. Smooth muscle works inside organs and blood vessels. Cardiac muscle forms the heart.

facts.title: Skin the Body’s Protective Cover
facts.body:
Skin is the body’s largest organ. It protects against injury, germs, and water loss. The skin helps regulate temperature and sense touch.

Layers of skin have different functions and cell types. Pigment, oil glands, and sweat glands all play important roles.

facts.title: The Stomach Begins Digestion
facts.body:
The stomach stores food and mixes it with acid and enzymes. Its muscular walls churn food into a semi-liquid mixture. Acid helps kill many microbes and unfold proteins.

Mucus protects the stomach lining from self-digestion. Digestion continues more fully in the small intestine.

facts.title: The Small Intestine Absorbs Nutrients
facts.body:
The small intestine is the main site of nutrient absorption. Its inner surface has folds, villi, and microvilli for extra area. Enzymes and bile help break food into absorbable pieces.

Nutrients pass into blood or lymph. Its long length helps the body capture as much nourishment as possible.

facts.title: The Liver Performs Silent Chemistry
facts.body:
The liver processes nutrients and many chemicals from digestion. It helps regulate blood sugar and stores energy. The liver makes bile for fat digestion.

It also helps break down toxins and old blood cells. This organ performs hundreds of important chemical tasks.

facts.title: Kidneys as Natural Filters
facts.body: The kidneys filter blood and balance water, salts, and wastes. They form urine by carefully reabsorbing needed substances. Kidneys also help regulate blood pressure. They produce signals involved in red blood cell production.

facts.title: The Eye Captures Light
facts.body:
The eye focuses light onto the retina. Photoreceptor cells convert light into nerve signals. The lens changes shape to help focus at different distances.

The iris controls how much light enters. Vision depends on both the eye and the brain.

facts.title: Ears Hear and Help Balance
facts.body: The ear detects sound and contributes to balance. The outer ear collects sound waves. The middle ear transmits vibration through tiny bones.

facts.title: The Immune System Defends the Body
facts.body: The immune system helps protect the body from harmful microbes and abnormal cells. It includes barriers, white blood cells, antibodies, and signaling molecules. Some defenses act quickly while others are highly specific.

facts.title: The Nervous System Sends Messages Fast
facts.body: The nervous system coordinates sensation, thought, and response. The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. Nerves reaching the body form the peripheral nervous system. Neurons send signals rapidly along specialized pathways.

facts.title: Hormones and the Endocrine System
facts.body:
Hormones are chemical messengers released into the blood. They help regulate growth, metabolism, stress, and reproduction. Glands such as the thyroid and pancreas produce important hormones.

Hormonal effects are often slower than nerve signals but longer lasting. The endocrine system helps maintain internal balance.

facts.title: DNA Inside Every Cell Nucleus
facts.body: The nucleus stores most of a cell’s DNA in many human cells. It helps control which genes are active. Genetic instructions guide protein production and cell behavior. DNA is packaged into chromosomes.

facts.title: The Human Microbiome
facts.body:
The human body hosts communities of helpful microbes. Many live on the skin and in the gut. These microbes can aid digestion and compete with harmful organisms.

They also interact with the immune system. A healthy microbiome is influenced by diet, environment, and habits.

facts.title: Teeth Built for Biting and Grinding
facts.body: Human teeth cut, tear, and grind food before swallowing. Enamel is the hardest substance in the body. Different tooth shapes have different jobs. Baby teeth are later replaced by most adult teeth.

facts.title: Sleep Repairs and Resets
facts.body:
Sleep is an active biological state rather than simple shutdown. During sleep the body and brain carry out repair and regulation. Sleep helps memory, mood, and attention.

People cycle through different stages including rapid eye movement sleep. Too little sleep can affect nearly every system.

facts.title: The Spinal Cord as Information Highway
facts.body:
The spinal cord carries signals between the brain and the body. It also helps control reflexes that happen very quickly. Protective bones called vertebrae surround it.

Different levels of the cord connect with different body regions. Damage there can disrupt movement and sensation.

facts.title: The Pancreas Balances Digestion and Sugar
facts.body:
The pancreas aids digestion and blood sugar control. It releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine. It also makes hormones including insulin and glucagon.

Those hormones help keep glucose levels in a healthy range. This small organ has both digestive and endocrine roles.

facts.title: Hair and Nails from Living Roots
facts.body: Hair and nails are made mostly of tough protein called keratin. Visible hair and nail portions are not living tissue. Growth comes from active cells at their base. Hair can help with protection and temperature regulation.

facts.title: Reflexes Faster Than Thought
facts.body:
A reflex is a rapid automatic response to a stimulus. Some reflexes are handled largely through the spinal cord. They help protect the body from injury.

Reflex testing can reveal nervous system function. These quick pathways show that not every response waits for full conscious processing.

facts.title: Growth from Childhood to Adulthood
facts.body:
Human growth involves cell division, hormones, nutrition, and genetics. Bones lengthen at growth plates during childhood. The brain and body mature at different speeds.

Puberty brings major physical and hormonal changes. Growth reflects both inherited traits and environmental conditions.

facts.title: Bones Are Living Tissue
facts.body: Bones are not static structures. They constantly remodel through cells that break down old bone and build new bone, helping the skeleton adapt to stress and repair tiny damage over time. Strength training, nutrition, and hormones all influence this cycle, which is why movement and diet matter for long-term bone health.

facts.title: Skin Is a Smart Barrier
facts.body: Skin protects against microbes, limits water loss, and helps regulate temperature. It also contains sensory receptors that detect pressure, pain, and heat in real time. Because skin performs many jobs at once, small changes like hydration, sleep, and sun exposure can affect both comfort and recovery.
